transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-02-08 16:00 UTC | Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Morgan (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Erin Patel (Mariner - Head of Platform), Carlos Reyes (Mariner - SRE), Maya Thompson (Mariner - Head of ML)

Summary (auto): quick walkthrough of Redwood Optimize: focus on batching and KV/prefix cache. Went through cost model examples, showed how batching gains vary by seq length and tail latency. Discussed Dedicated vs hosted and security controls. Next: pricing and benchmark.

[00:00] Aisha: hey everyone, thanks for joining, you should have the deck I shared, um Liam will run through Optimize recommendations for batching and caching and then we can map that back to your traffic, does that sound good?
[00:08] Erin: yep sounds good, thanks Aisha. we've got about 50 minutes. we're especially interested in p95 latency at peak, and costs — right now we're mostly self-hosted 8xA100 and it's expensive.
[00:18] Liam: cool, quick intro, i'm Liam, infra/serving SE at Redwood. we'll start high-level: batching gives per-token cost reduction at the expense of queueing latency; prefix cache and KV cache reduce compute by avoiding re-computation of prefixes or recurrent KV loads.
[00:35] Carlos: quick question, when you say prefix cache, is that same as KV cache? we call it KV cache in-house and sometimes prefix caching confuses folks.
[00:44] Liam: yeah great q — shorthand causes confusion. prefix caching is storing common prompt prefixes (e.g., system prompts, user history snippets) and reusing their activations downstream; KV cache is the key-value attention cache for ongoing generation. both help but in different patterns — prefix cache reduces initial encoder work, KV cache avoids regen on continuation.
[01:05] Maya: our average seq length on completions is around 320 tokens, but we have a long-tail with some at 2k. p95 target is 120ms server-side for interactive flows.
[01:14] Erin: and our QPS at peak is about 60 rps for chat flows, peaks to 120 during flash times.
[01:22] Liam: ok that's helpful. i'll demo a cost model: baseline hosted single-request no batching, then small-batch (2-4), medium (8-16), and large (32+). note: batching efficiency depends on sequence length distribution and our batching window (we default 10-20ms but can be tuned).
[01:40] [screen share noise] Liam: slide 3 — here's an example: for 320 token median, moving from batch1 -> batch8 yields ~2.8x throughput improvement and ~35-45% cost reduction per token; p95 latency goes up modestly if your batching window is high. with a 10ms batching window you typically keep p95 within your 120ms if tail sequences are capped or you use early-exit.
[02:05] Carlos: so the tradeoff is queueing delay, right? if we need strict 50ms p95 we can't batch much.
[02:12] Liam: correct. there's also continuous batching — it's more efficient because it aggregates in-flight requests across model instances. Redwood supports adaptive batching tied to SLOs so you can set latency max and the runtime will try to honor it.
[02:26] Aisha: worth noting: for Dedicated customers we can set node pools and autoscale so you get predictable throughput without noisy neighbors, and the Optimize tool will suggest batch sizes per route.
[02:36] Maya: can you walk through prefix cache example? we have a lot of repeated system prompts and user history snippets.
[02:42] Liam: sure. prefix cache is best when you have repeated or shared preambles. we store the model activations for the prefix and then reuse them — that can cut computation for prefixes by up to 70% depending on prefix length. for Mariner, if your average prefix is ~80 tokens and it's repeated across 40% of requests, we'd expect a 12-15% net cost reduction just from prefix caching.
[03:05] Erin: interesting — and how does that interact with KV cache?
[03:09] Liam: so KV cache is per-request generation state — it helps long-running conversations by avoiding re-computing attention for prior tokens each generation step. prefix cache is more like memoization of the prompt encoding. you can use both; they compound. the cost model slide shows combined savings.
[03:24] [08:00] Liam: jumping ahead — here's a live-ish cost table: current self-hosted estimated unit cost ~ $0.45 per 1k tokens (back-of-envelope), hosted Redwood naive no-opt ~ $0.55 per 1k, but with batching + prefix + KV cache we estimate down to $0.18-$0.22 per 1k tokens depending on batch targets and cache hit rates. these are example numbers — actual will vary.
[03:50] Carlos: those numbers look promising. what's the assumed GPU family? A100? M60?
[03:57] Liam: example uses A100 40GB; we also have quantized variants on 80GB and Hopper-like instances — profiling will pick the best kernel. Dedicated customers can pick instance types.
[04:10] Maya: if we use prefix cache do we need to change app flow? like do we need to pin keys or manage TTLs?
[04:16] Liam: good point — you expose a cache key or Redwood can compute a deterministic key from prompt fingerprints. TTLs are configurable; we recommend 5-30 minutes for conversational prefixes but it depends. for privacy you can choose ephemeral keys or per-tenant scoping.
[04:33] Erin: data residency and KMS are big for us. will your hosted logs ever contain plaintext prompts? we need SOC2 + key management details.
[04:41] Aisha: yep, we can share SOC2 + sec whitepaper after this call. Hosted keeps minimal logs by default; for sensitive flows we recommend Dedicated private with customer-managed KMS and optional on-prem package. we'll send the network architecture + KMS notes.
[04:58] [12:30] Liam: back to batching: a practical recommendation — set latency SLO target (you're at 120ms p95). set initial batching window 10ms, target batch size 8 for median seq 320. enable prefix cache for common templates and KV cache by default for conversation flows. that combination tends to hit both cost and latency targets.
[05:18] Carlos: how do you measure cache hit rates? we need observability to see when cache is being effective.
[05:24] Liam: Redwood Console gives per-route cache hit metrics, token-level cost, and p95 latency. we'll also expose traces so you can correlate hits with lower latency.
[05:33] Maya: curious about long tails — our 2k token requests will blow up latency. any advice?
[05:38] Liam: for tail-heavy workloads we recommend hybrid routing: route long sequences to a high-memory Dedicated pool with slightly higher cost but better p95, and route short interactive flows to low-latency pool. Redwood Optimize can suggest split thresholds based on your histogram.
[05:55] Erin: is routing automatic or we need to implement in app?
[06:00] Liam: you can configure routing policies in the Console by condition (seq_length, route, customer_tier). Redwood handles it in the control plane; your app sends metadata (estimated length or prompt fingerprint) and we route.
[06:12] Aisha: also worth noting model fallbacks — if a variant is down we fall back to a compatible quantized model to avoid failures.
[06:19] [20:00] Liam: demo time — here's a short benchmark run we did with a similar fintech profile: QPS 80, median seq 340, batch8 window 12ms, p95 110ms, cost per 1k tokens $0.20.
[06:35] Carlos: what's the cost math: where does the savings come from?
[06:38] Liam: mostly from utilization: batching increases tokens/sec per GPU by packing sequences, prefix caches remove rework, and KV cache removes generation overhead. the cost model slide breaks it: GPU cost / effective tokens/sec, minus cache savings.
[06:50] Maya: would you be able to run a benchmark against our traces? we could scrub and share.
[06:55] Liam: yes, we do a 2-hour benchmark as part of POC scoping. we need anonymized traces and expected SLOs. we'll provide a plan and test harness.
[07:03] Erin: timeline-wise, we want a POC in March and procurement loop closes early April, ideally.
[07:09] Aisha: that sounds feasible. we'll get you pricing and a POC plan this week.
[07:14] [30:00] Carlos: two operational Qs: how do you handle cache invalidation for user context when users update profile info mid-conversation?
[07:20] Liam: good one — you can attach cache keys to context versioning. when a user mutates data, you bump the context version and the cache miss triggers re-encode. Redwood supports tag-based invalidation hooks and TTLs.
[07:32] Mara (sic) [transcription mislabel]: and encryption at rest for cached activations?
[07:36] Aisha: yes, all customer data at rest is encrypted; for Dedicated you can use customer-managed keys and HSM if needed. we'll attach the KMS doc.
[07:44] Maya: any gotchas with function/tool calling and caching? we call external APIs during prompt construction.
[07:50] Liam: function calls complicate prefix caching if the call-dependent content is in the prefix; you want to separate static templates vs dynamic outputs so static parts can be cached. we often recommend templating so the dynamic bits are appended post-cache.
[07:59] Erin: can you share the exact metrics you need in the traces? we want to prepare a scrubbed bundle.
[08:04] Liam: we'll send a trace template — need timestamped prompts, seq lengths, QPS by route, and a sample of long-tail examples. nothing PII.
[08:12] Carlos: ok great. what about SLA and uptime for Dedicated?
[08:16] Aisha: Dedicated comes with an SLA (we commit to 99.9% uptime for the cluster and latency targets vary by plan). we'll include the SLA doc in the pack.
[08:24] Maya: one more — do you do automated quantization suggestions? we saw in docs something about quant profiles per workload.
[08:30] Liam: yes, Optimize recommends quantization/precision based on evals; it will recommend full float for latency-sensitive or high-quality flows and int8/4-bit for cost sensitive ones with quality checks.
[08:40] [45:00] Aisha: quick recap: - we'll send pricing + Dedicated estimate, security pack (SOC2, KMS, network), and a benchmark plan. - Mariner will send anonymized traces + target SLOs. - schedule POC scoping 2027-02-17. any objections?
[08:58] Erin: no objections, sounds good. excited to see numbers vs our current infra.
[09:05] Carlos: thanks, looking forward to benchmark.
[09:10] Aisha: great, we'll follow up by email. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

Notes: occasional transcription errors in speaker labels and timestamps. References in call to Dedicated, Optimize, prefix cache, KV cache, batching window, and Console. Links shared: /docs/optimize/benchmark-plan (note: placeholder), /docs/security/soc2.pdf (placeholder).
